Do the following using the steps provided in their respective sections.
        Steps:
        1. clone the repo git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
        2. analyse the contents of the repo and create following.
            2.1 create/update dockerfile based on the analysis. 
            2.2 kubernetes yamls based on the analysis.
            2.3 github actions file to build application on pushing to main branch.
        3. add all changed file to git changes

function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: Generates a Dockerfile in the specified repository directory with a default configuration. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the repository directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory name within the filesystem.

base_image.description: The base image to use in the Dockerfile. For example, 'python:3.8-slim'.

maintainer.description: The maintainer information to be added to the Dockerfile. Format should be 'Name <email@example.com>'.

port.description: The port number that the container will expose. For example, '80' for a web server.

commands.description: Additional commands to be executed when building the image, separated by ';'. For example, 'apt-get update; apt-get install -y git'.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be a valid path relative to the project root.

deployment_name.description: The name to assign to the Kubernetes deployment. This name must be unique within the Kubernetes namespace.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to use for the deployment. This should include the repository name and tag, if applicable, in the format 'repository/image:tag'.

replicas.description: The number of instances to deploy for the specified Docker image.

service_type.description: The type of service to create for the deployment. Typical values include 'ClusterIP', 'NodePort', and 'LoadBalancer'.

port.description: The port number that the service should expose. This should correspond to the port that the application inside the Docker container is set to listen on.

target_port.description: The target port on the pod to which the service will send requests. This should be the same as the port that the application inside the Docker container is set to listen on.

function.name: analyse_repo_contents
function.description: Analyzes the contents of a repository to determine the predominant programming language used within. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the repository is located. This should be the root directory of the repository.

include_subdirectories.description: A flag indicating whether to include subdirectories in the analysis. If set to true, all subdirectories will be recursively analyzed.

excluded_files.description: An array of file names or patterns to exclude from the analysis, such as ['README.md', '*.txt'].

language_threshold.description: The percentage threshold for a language to be considered predominant in the repository. This should be a value between 0 and 100. This is a float type value.

`git push origin main` | --- ## 1. Clone the Repository ```bash git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git cd nodejs-welcome ``` --- ## 2. Analyse the Repository Run the following function to get an overview of the languages used. (If you’re running this in a notebook or script that has the `functions` namespace available.) ```python from functions import analyse_repo_contents analysis_result = analyse_repo_contents( directory_name="nodejs-welcome", include_subdirectories=True, excluded_files=["README.md"], language_threshold=10.0 ) print(analysis_result) ``` > **Note:** The result will contain a `predominant_language` field. For a typical Node.js project, you’ll likely see `"JavaScript"` or `"TypeScript"`. --- ## 3. Create/Update Dockerfile Assuming the predominant language is JavaScript (Node.js), run: ```python from functions import create_a_docker_file dockerfile_result = create_a_docker_file( directory_name="nodejs-welcome", base_image="node:18-alpine", maintainer="Your Name ", port=3000, commands="npm install; npm run build" ) print(dockerfile_result) ``` This will generate a `Dockerfile` similar to: ```dockerfile FROM node:18-alpine LABEL maintainer="Your Name " WORKDIR /app COPY package*.json ./ RUN npm install COPY . . EXPOSE 3000 CMD ["npm", "start"] ``` --- ## 4. Create Kubernetes YAMLs ```python from functions import create_kubernetes_yaml_file k8s_result = create_kubernetes_yaml_file( directory_name="nodejs-welcome", deployment_name="nodejs-welcome-deployment", image_name="your-docker-repo/nodejs-welcome:latest", replicas=3, service_type="ClusterIP", port=80, target_port=3000 ) print(k8s_result) ``` This will produce two files: * `deployment.yaml` * `service.yaml` Example `deployment.yaml`: ```yaml apiVersion: apps/v1 kind: Deployment metadata: name: nodejs-welcome-deployment spec: replicas: 3 selector: matchLabels: app: nodejs-welcome template: metadata: labels: app: nodejs-welcome spec: containers: - name: nodejs-welcome image: your-docker-repo/nodejs-welcome:latest ports: - containerPort: 3000 ``` Example `service.yaml`: ```yaml apiVersion: v1 kind: Service metadata: name: nodejs-welcome-service spec: type: ClusterIP selector: app: nodejs-welcome ports: - protocol: TCP port: 80 targetPort: 3000 ``` --- ## 5. Create GitHub Actions Workflow Create a file at `.github/workflows/build.yml` with the following content: ```yaml name: Build and Deploy on: push: branches: - main jobs: build: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v3 - name: Set up Node.js uses: actions/setup-node@v3 with: node-version: '18' - name: Install dependencies run: npm ci - name: Run tests run: npm test - name: Build Docker image run: | docker build -t your-docker-repo/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }} . echo ${{ secrets.DOCKER_PASSWORD }} | docker login -u ${{ secrets.DOCKER_USERNAME }} --password-stdin docker push your-docker-repo/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }} - name: Deploy to Kubernetes env: KUBECONFIG: ${{ secrets.KUBECONFIG }} run: | kubectl set image deployment/nodejs-welcome-deployment nodejs-welcome=your-docker-repo/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }} kubectl rollout status deployment/nodejs-welcome-deployment ``` > **Important:** Replace `your-docker-repo` with your actual Docker registry/repository name. Also, make sure you’ve added the following secrets to your GitHub repository: > * `DOCKER_USERNAME` > * `DOCKER_PASSWORD` > * `KUBECONFIG` (if you’re deploying to a cluster that requires a kubeconfig) --- ## 6. Stage, Commit, and Push Changes ```bash git add Dockerfile deployment.yaml service.yaml .github/workflows/build.yml git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and CI workflow" git push origin main ``` That’s it! Once you push, GitHub Actions will automatically build the Docker image, push it to your registry, and deploy it to your Kubernetes cluster.
